Radar Cross-Section (RCS) quantifies an object's visibility to radar by measuring backscattered power relative to incident power.
Antennas inherently increase platform RCS due to their metallic and radiating nature, conflicting with stealth requirements.
Three antenna models were designed and analyzed: baseline (Model A), geometrically optimized (Model B), and hybrid with RAM and FSS (Model C).
Model A had a -10 dB return loss bandwidth from 3.1 to 4.8 GHz with a resonant frequency at 3.9 GHz.
Model B improved bandwidth to 3.8–6.0 GHz by adding edge curvature and serration, enhancing impedance matching and reducing reflections.
Model C extended bandwidth further to 3.5–7.8 GHz using a Frequency Selective Surface and Radar Absorbing Material.
The baseline antenna showed a peak RCS of about +3 dBsm at 5 GHz, indicating high radar visibility.
Model B reduced RCS to approximately -8 dBsm in the 4–8 GHz range by scattering incident waves in non-specular directions.
Model C achieved a minimum RCS of -15 dBsm at 5 GHz, representing an 80% reduction compared to the baseline.
RAM converts incident electromagnetic energy into heat, reducing reflected radar signals.
FSS layers selectively reflect or transmit waves to reduce backscatter and improve antenna stealth.
The hybrid antenna maintained constant gain and directivity despite slight radiation efficiency loss.
Simulation used CST Microwave Studio employing FEM, FDTD, and MoM techniques for electromagnetic analysis.
Return loss (S11) below -10 dB indicates good impedance matching and efficient radiation.
Surface current distribution analysis showed that geometric shaping disrupts uniform currents, reducing coherent backscatter.
Active RCS control methods involve tunable materials and components for adaptive stealth but were not the focus here.
The study fills a gap by analyzing broadband (2–12 GHz) antenna RCS reduction combining materials and geometry.
Stealth technology traditionally focuses on airframe shaping and RAM, but antenna RCS is a critical overlooked factor.
The hybrid antenna design supports applications in satellite communication, radar, Wi-Fi, and microwave relays.
The research suggests future integration of metamaterials and machine learning for intelligent RCS control.
